craft_claim: Repeated false or exaggerated alarms desensitize audiences, so later genuine warnings draw weaker response (crying wolf / alarm fatigue).

supporting_evidence.location: Cry Wolf: The Psychology of False Alarms, book thesis
supporting_evidence.note: Breznitz's study of false alarms argues that erroneous warnings impose psychological costs and degrade response to subsequent true warnings; the cost is not only wasted attention but reduced credibility.

supporting_evidence.location: Sentinel Event Alert, Issue 50 (medical device alarm safety)
supporting_evidence.note: Institutional recognition that staff become desensitized to frequent alarms, including false ones, and may ignore or fail to respond to critical signals. This is the operational form of crying wolf.

counterevidence.note: Repetition and confirmation are not uniformly harmful: repeated accurate warnings can strengthen response. The damage is done specifically by false or exaggerated alarms, not by repetition as such.

scope: Any channel that issues warnings or urgency claims repeatedly to the same audience.
exceptions: The false-alarm penalty is smaller when audiences understand the uncertainty and the cost of missed warnings.
Effect sizes and mechanisms vary by domain and are not uniform across all warning systems.
